newsitem.title: USA: Grigsby Brandford shake-up follows controversies.
newsitem.headline: Grigsby Brandford shake-up follows controversies.

text.p: Calvin B. Grigsby has resigned as chairman of San Francisco-based Grigsby Brandford & Co, one of the nation's largest minority-owned investment banking firms, the company said on Tuesday.

The move came a week after California state officials disclosed that Grigsby paid a $5,000 fine for making campaign gifts in the state without full disclosure. It also followed problems with a Cleveland bond deal in late August.
After news of Grigsby's resignation, several local government finance officials expressed surprise.
"It's surprising," said San Francisco's director of public finance, Laura Wagner-Lockwood. "We'll just have to wait to see what it's really about."

Walter Knorr, Chicago's chief financial officer, said he would monitor the firm's performance in future deals to determine if Grigsby's departure will cause any "philosophical changes" in the firm's trading and sales capabilities.
"We will have to keep tabs on them," Knorr said.
Grigsby, the long-time chairman of the minority-owned firm he founded in 1981, could not be reached for comment.
In a news release, Grigsby said that he was "looking forward to this as a major intersection in my life after a career devoted primarily to Grigsby Brandford & Co."
"I'm proud of Grigsby Brandford, the contribution it has made, and I'm eager to pursue new opportunities at this stage in my life," he said.

The investment banking and financial advisory firm underwrites, sells and trades municipal bonds, preferred stock, Treasury notes and other government securities. It is the only black-owned investment bank to rank in the top 15 senior managers of tax-exempt financial deals.

As part of the realignment at the firm this week, Napoleon Brandford was appointed to chairman of the board by the private firm's shareholders. Suzanne Shank, a managing director for Grigsby Brandford based in the Midwest, was named president and chief executive officer.
Earlier this month, the California Fair Political Practices Commission said Grigsby had paid a $5,000 fine for making campaign contributions without full and complete disclosure.
In an interview last week, Grigsby said the press was exaggerating the campaign contribution violations.
"I don't consider this a major item. To me, it's not a big deal because it's just a reporting violation," he said. "Somehow, the press has made it look a lot more than that."
"Why that happens, I think, has a lot to do with their interest in the fact that I'm an African-American," Grigsby said. "I think there's some character assassination there."
Separately, undisclosed problems in August stopped Grigsby's firm from signing a purchase agreement for $82 million of Cleveland parking facilities refunding revenue bonds.
The lack of an agreement forced Cleveland to scrap the deal and return to the market a week later with Smith Barney Inc as the bookrunner and Grigsby Brandford reduced to a co-manager spot.
Market conditions worsened during the week that pricing was delayed, shaving $500,000 off the $7.5 million present value savings for the deal, a Cleveland official said afterwards.
